diagnostic_probe: After collecting like terms, does a nonzero squared term remain?
domain: Real coefficients; classify after collecting like powers.
explanation: A polynomial is quadratic exactly when its collected x^2 coefficient is nonzero.
hint: Start by expanding brackets and collecting the powers of the variable.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply standard form and degree after simplification

subject: mathematics
title: Standard form and degree after simplification

diagnostic_probe: Which sign belongs to the linear coefficient?
domain: Real signed coefficients, including zero coefficients.
explanation: Keep coefficient signs when moving terms to one side and collecting powers.
hint: Rewrite subtraction as addition of a signed term before reading coefficients.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply signed coefficients

subject: mathematics
title: Signed coefficients

diagnostic_probe: What value does the original left-hand side have at your proposed root?
domain: Real x and real candidate r.
explanation: Substitute a candidate into the original polynomial. A zero remainder certifies that candidate, but completeness needs all roots.
hint: Substitute the proposed value before deciding whether it is a root.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply roots verified by substitution

subject: mathematics
title: Roots verified by substitution

diagnostic_probe: Could either factor be zero, rather than just the first?
domain: Real factors. No division by a possibly zero factor.
explanation: A product of two real factors is zero only when at least one factor is zero. Check both factors; retain a possible zero root.
hint: Keep both factors visible and ask what makes each one vanish.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply factorisation and zero-product reasoning

subject: mathematics
title: Factorisation and zero-product reasoning

diagnostic_probe: What separate value comes from each sign in the numerator?
domain: a != 0; D >= 0; c=(b^2-D)/(4*a). Distinct values only.
explanation: The two quadratic-formula branches are (-b+sqrt(D))/(2*a) and (-b-sqrt(D))/(2*a); D=0 gives one distinct value. Keep sqrt(D) symbolic when an exact answer is requested; a rounded decimal is an approximation.
hint: Write one line for the plus branch and another for the minus branch.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply quadratic formula and both branches

subject: mathematics
title: Quadratic formula and both branches

diagnostic_probe: Are you using the discriminant to count real roots or to name their values?
domain: a != 0; real coefficients; D=b^2-4*a*c.
explanation: D>0 gives two distinct real roots, D=0 one repeated real root, D<0 no real roots. Completing the square reduces the equation to (2*a*x+b)^2=D.
hint: Classify the sign of the discriminant before attempting to extract a square root.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply discriminant and real-root classification

subject: mathematics
title: Discriminant and real-root classification

diagnostic_probe: What does your variable represent, and which quantities depend on it?
domain: Rectangle: width>0, width+gap>0. Travel: v>r>0; distance and delay positive.
explanation: Translate the actual constraints before solving. Rectangle area is w*(w+g). Travel delay is L/(v-r)-L/v; clearing denominators retains v>r.
hint: Write the relationships in words first, then replace each quantity with an expression.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply constructing a quadratic model

subject: mathematics
title: Constructing a quadratic model

diagnostic_probe: Which roots satisfy the units and restrictions of the story?
domain: Original context and all denominator restrictions apply after algebra.
explanation: Discard algebraic roots that violate dimensions, speeds or original denominators. Squaring and clearing denominators do not erase the original restrictions.
hint: Keep algebraic solving separate from the final context check.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply admissible roots in context

subject: mathematics
title: Admissible roots in context

diagnostic_probe: Do consecutive terms change by the same amount?
domain: Observed finite sequence; at least three terms for a multiple-difference test.
explanation: An AP has the same forward difference at each adjacent pair. A familiar pattern alone does not establish an AP.
hint: Calculate several neighbouring differences rather than looking only at the first pair.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply recognising constant successive differences

subject: mathematics
title: Recognising constant successive differences

diagnostic_probe: What happens to the sign if the subtraction order is reversed?
domain: a,d real; d may be positive, zero or negative.
explanation: The first term is a. Common difference is later minus earlier for adjacent terms; decreasing and constant APs are allowed.
hint: Use later term minus earlier term consistently.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply first term and signed common difference

subject: mathematics
title: First term and signed common difference

diagnostic_probe: How many jumps take you from term one to term n?
domain: n is a positive integer; a,d real.
explanation: Term n is a+(n-1)*d: there are n-1 jumps. The recurrence starts at a and adds d once per next position.
hint: Check your expression at n=1 before using it for another position.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply nth term

subject: mathematics
title: Nth term

diagnostic_probe: Are you counting positions or the gaps between them?
domain: m,n positive integer indices.
explanation: Term n minus term m is (n-m)*d. Inclusive term count includes both endpoints: end-start+1.
hint: Sketch a short sequence and label both term numbers and gaps.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply indexing and displacement between terms

subject: mathematics
title: Indexing and displacement between terms

diagnostic_probe: Does the position you calculated correspond to an actual term number?
domain: d != 0 for inversion; the resulting index must be a positive integer. If d=0, only a occurs.
explanation: Solve n=1+(value-a)/d, then enforce the discrete index domain. Algebraic fractional or nonpositive n is not membership.
hint: After solving for n, check positivity and integrality.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply membership and integer term numbers

subject: mathematics
title: Membership and integer term numbers

diagnostic_probe: Does the task ask for one term or the total up to that term?
domain: n positive integer; sum means cumulative total, not term n.
explanation: S_n=n*(2*a+(n-1)*d)/2. The base case is S_1=a; S_n-S_(n-1) equals the nth term, proving the formula by induction. Reversing the AP pairs term k with term n+1-k: each pair totals 2*a+(n-1)*d=a+last. Adding the forward and reversed sums gives 2*S_n=n*(a+last).
hint: Name the quantity you want before selecting a formula.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply sum of the first n terms

subject: mathematics
title: Sum of the first n terms

diagnostic_probe: What cancels when you subtract the equations for two known terms?
domain: Known indices m != n; both positive integers.
explanation: Recover d=(term_n-term_m)/(n-m), then a=term_n-(n-1)*d. Three consecutive AP terms have arithmetic mean in the middle.
hint: Write the two term equations with the same a before subtracting.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply recovering ap parameters from constraints

subject: mathematics
title: Recovering AP parameters from constraints

diagnostic_probe: Is the change a fixed addition, and what exactly is being accumulated?
domain: Finite n positive integer; consistent cumulative records.
explanation: Use S_n=n*(a+last)/2 for a finite AP, and term n=S_n-S_(n-1). An inverse sum may admit more than one positive count.
hint: List the first few quantities with units and identify the requested output.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply ap modelling and finite sums

subject: mathematics
title: AP modelling and finite sums

diagnostic_probe: Which angle is the reference, and which side is opposite it?
domain: Positive right triangle, other two angles acute.
explanation: Opposite and adjacent depend on the reference angle. Swapping the two acute angles exchanges these sides while keeping the hypotenuse.
hint: Mark the right angle and the reference angle before naming sides.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply triangle sides relative to a reference angle

subject: mathematics
title: Triangle sides relative to a reference angle

diagnostic_probe: Which pair of sides defines the ratio you chose?
domain: Positive sides o,a,h; o^2+a^2=h^2; acute angle.
explanation: sin=o/h, cos=a/h, tan=o/a, sec=h/a, csc=h/o, cot=a/o. Identify the reference angle before choosing sides.
hint: Write the side-ratio definition before inserting numbers.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply six trigonometric ratios

subject: mathematics
title: Six trigonometric ratios

diagnostic_probe: Which ratio is actually paired with sine as its reciprocal?
domain: Ratios only on their original domains; acute angles make all six finite.
explanation: Reciprocals: sin*csc=1, cos*sec=1, tan*cot=1. Quotients: tan=sin/cos and cot=cos/sin.
hint: Use the side definitions to derive the reciprocal instead of guessing from the names.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply reciprocal and quotient relationships

subject: mathematics
title: Reciprocal and quotient relationships

diagnostic_probe: What happens to a side ratio when both lengths are multiplied by the same factor?
domain: Positive common scale k and positive original side lengths.
explanation: Scaling all triangle sides by the same positive factor leaves the side ratios unchanged.
hint: Keep the common scaling factor in numerator and denominator and cancel it.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply scale invariance of ratios

subject: mathematics
title: Scale invariance of ratios

diagnostic_probe: Can the special triangle give an exact ratio before decimal calculation?
domain: Degrees in {0,30,45,60,90}; explicit endpoint domain checks.
explanation: Use exact special-triangle ratios and explicit undefined entries. Standard-angle values are exhaustively checked against a second route. Exact values for angles [0,30,45,60,90] degrees, in that order: sin=[0,1/2,1/sqrt(2),sqrt(3)/2,1]; cos=[1,sqrt(3)/2,1/sqrt(2),1/2,0]; tan=[0,1/sqrt(3),1,sqrt(3),undefined]; sec=[1,2/sqrt(3),sqrt(2),2,undefined]; csc=[undefined,2,sqrt(2),2/sqrt(3),1]; cot=[undefined,sqrt(3),1,1/sqrt(3),0]. Here csc means cosec.
hint: Identify the standard angle and recall or reconstruct its special triangle.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply exact ratios at standard angles

subject: mathematics
title: Exact ratios at standard angles

diagnostic_probe: What is the denominator of the ratio at this angle?
domain: Evaluate the original expression before cancellation; a zero denominator is excluded.
explanation: A ratio with a zero denominator is undefined, never zero or infinity. Cancelling identical expressions does not restore excluded angles.
hint: Evaluate the denominator separately before dividing.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply defined and undefined endpoint ratios

subject: mathematics
title: Defined and undefined endpoint ratios

diagnostic_probe: Does the angle value represent degrees, and where does the square apply?
domain: Angles supplied in degrees; trig functions in the checker take radians.
explanation: Radians=degrees*pi/180. sin^2(theta) means (sin(theta))^2. The square applies to the value, not to the angle.
hint: Write the degree symbol or convert explicitly, and add brackets around the quantity being squared.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply angle units and notation

subject: mathematics
title: Angle units and notation

diagnostic_probe: Which identity matches the squared ratios in your expression?
domain: Identity is valid on the common domain; sec/tan require cos!=0, csc/cot require sin!=0.
explanation: sin^2+cos^2=1; sec^2-tan^2=1; csc^2-cot^2=1. Retain the original domain when simplifying.
hint: Rewrite the expression using one known identity while retaining denominator restrictions.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply pythagorean trigonometric identities

subject: mathematics
title: Pythagorean trigonometric identities

diagnostic_probe: Would checking a single angle establish the claim for every allowed angle?
domain: Universal claim over every acute angle; counterexamples must be finite and in-domain.
explanation: Symbolic reasoning establishes an identity on its domain. One matching angle cannot prove it; one valid counterexample can disprove it.
hint: Use side definitions or known identities to transform expressions symbolically.

learning_outcome.description: Explain and apply identity reasoning versus a numerical example

subject: mathematics
title: Identity reasoning versus a numerical example
